lore.summary: The landshark. A great armoured brute that swims through soil as a shark swims water, with only a ridged crest cutting the surface to warn you it is coming. It feels your footfalls long before it surfaces, comes up beneath the middle of a marching column, and takes whatever it lands among. Ploughland, downs, and any road with soft ground beside it.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — larger than a cart-horse and half again as broad, all plate and jaw.
Durability: Immense. It is built like a siege engine and takes wounding like one.
Defenses: Overlapping bony plates from snout to tail; a spear-thrust turns unless it finds a seam. It has no cunning, and does not appear to need any.
Speed: Alarmingly quick on the surface, and slow beneath it — but underground it need not hurry, because it always knows exactly where you are standing.
Might: Four raking claws and jaws that shear through mail and the man inside it. Worse, it leaps: it will throw its whole weight into the air and land upon a man with all four sets of claws working at once.
Mind: A beast, and barely that. Appetite with armour on.
Disposition: Perpetually, stupidly hungry, and afraid of nothing that walks.
Bane: It hunts by the shaking of the ground and by almost nothing else. Get off the earth — onto bare rock it cannot chew, up a wall, onto a wagon bed, into a boat — and it loses you entirely and casts about like a blind dog. It swims through soil only. Stone stops it dead.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It circles beneath you first, reading your steps, then erupts under the worst place it can find and bites. Scatter and it takes the nearest; cluster and it leaps — up and over the front rank to land among the soft ones behind. It does not manoeuvre and it does not retreat. It goes under again only to come up somewhere better.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Fight it on stone. On soft ground you are fighting on its terms and you will bury people.
• It refuses to eat elves and turns its nose up at dwarf-meat — but it will still kill you either way. Do not stake your life on being unappetising.
• It loves halfling and horse above all other meat. Picket the animals well away from where your people sleep.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: None. I have spoken civilly with far worse-looking things than this and been answered, but there is nobody at all behind that snout. It will not eat an elf and it dislikes dwarves — that is the entirety of its philosophy, and it will bite you in half while it settles the question.

lore.summary: Swamp-born and swamp-hearted, the black is the cruellest of the chromatic breed. It lies drowned to the eyes in stagnant water among the cypress roots, waiting; it breathes a searing spray that strips flesh from bone; and it fouls whole meres out of pure spite, that a village downstream may thirst. Where the reeds go silent, look up.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge by its middle years — a long-necked serpent-thing on four legs, and the eldest are longer than a river barge.
Durability: Vast vigour; it fights on through wounds that would drop a bull mammoth and keep it down.
Defenses: Pitted black scale that turns honest steel; older ones want enchanted arms before they will mark, and the eldest shrug off spellcraft outright.
Speed: Lumbering afoot, tireless on the wing, and faster through black water than any boat you own.
Might: Bite, raking claws, a tail like a felled tree — and the acid, loosed in a long straight line that eats shield, mail and face together.
Mind: Sharp and well-spoken, and in its later years it wields a sorcerer's craft; it plans, it lies, and it remembers a slight for a lifetime.
Disposition: The most vile-tempered of all the coloured wyrms. It kills for sport, torments for amusement, and rules its fen by terror alone.
Bane: Acid is wasted on it — carry fire or frost. Drag it from its water and it fights clumsily afoot. And it is vain past all reason: flattery opens its mouth wider than any blade you carry.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It fights from ambush and never once fairly. Submerged to the nostrils, or coiled in a flooded ruin, it waits until you are wading and slow, then the terror of it strikes first and the acid comes down the line of your column. After that it takes to the air: a pass, a raking of claws, gone into the mist, back from another quarter. It will drown a heavy man rather than trade honest blows with him, and it hunts the weakest of a party first, for the pleasure of the rest watching.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Never parley standing in water. That is not a conversation, it is a table laid.
• The spray comes as a line, not a spreading cloud. Scatter wide and half its wrath falls on nothing.
• Flatter it. Every black I met would sooner be admired than fed, and admiring costs you nothing at all.

sections.title: Parley (wary)

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: A wyrmling black is a spiteful lizard the length of a man, spitting a thin jet of acid and hiding from herons in the reeds. With the passing spans it lengthens, the horns curl back from the skull, and the glossy hide dulls to pitted slate. The jet becomes a lance of ruin that will not spread and so must be dodged sideways. Cunning comes early to this breed and never leaves it. In the middle years it wraps itself in a darkness of its own making, its presence alone sets brave men running, and it begins to work true spells. The old ones command the swamp itself, calling up choking vines and plagues of biting flies; the very greatest can bid every crawling reptile in the fen rise against you. Judge the one before you by its horns and its eyes: a young one's horns are stubs and a ring of colour still shows around the pupil, while in the eldest the horns are a crown and the eyes have burned down to pits of smoke. lore.summary: Bronze wyrms keep the sea-cliffs, in halls whose only door lies beneath the tide. They are lawful to the bone, lovers of justice, and curious past all sense about the doings of small folk — so they walk among us in borrowed shapes: an old fisherman, a gull, a hound at a war-camp fire. Their breath is a bar of white lightning.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge in its prime — a ribbed, frilled wyrm the colour of a temple bell, and greater still with age.
Durability: Immense. It will outlast a whole company and be no worse for the morning.
Defenses: Metal-hard scale; the elder ones will not bleed for anything but enchanted steel, and the eldest turn spells aside like sea-spray.
Speed: Strong on the wing and a swimmer without equal — it breathes water as easily as air and can stay down as long as it pleases.
Might: A lance of lightning down a straight line, and a second breath few expect: a gas that unmans you outright and sends you stumbling away from the fight.
Mind: Keen, curious and better lettered than most sages. It speaks many tongues and takes plain delight in using them.
Disposition: Honourable, just, fond of company and dangerously fond of watching wars. It will judge you before it ever fights you.
Bane: Lightning is nothing to it and no water will drown it — what can be used is its honour. It keeps a bargain, it will not strike a man who has yielded, and it can be shamed into standing down. Mind also that the stranger at your elbow may be the wyrm; say nothing you would not say to its face.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It gives warning, and it means the warning. Press on and the lightning comes first, straight down your rank, then the gas that scatters whoever kept their feet, so that it may deal with the stubborn few at leisure. It fights from the air and from the surf, favours seizing and dropping a man in deep water over killing him, and it will not pursue those who run. But it kills what it has judged, without heat and without hurry, and it does not tire.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Any stranger on that coast might be him. Be civil to gulls, and to beggars.
• The lightning runs in a straight line. Do not stand in a column. Do not stand in the surf either.
• It will not break its word, so give yours only if you mean it. They remember for centuries.

sections.title: Parley (open)
sections.body: Talk first, always. I drank two nights with a fisherman on that coast who proved to be the very wyrm I had come to find; he laughed, forgave the errand, and gave me the road to what I actually wanted. Speak plainly, ask its opinion, keep any promise you make, and you leave richer than you came.

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: A bronze wyrmling comes from the shell already polite, dull as an old coin, ribbed of skull and frilled at the jaw, breathing the sea as readily as the air. Young, it learns the trick that shapes its whole long life — it puts on the shape of a beast or a man and walks off to learn something. As it grows the hide brightens toward true bell-metal with a green cast, the spark of its breath draws out into a lance, and it gains the arts of its kind: a meal conjured from nothing, a bank of fog, the reading of the thought behind your words before you speak them. The old ones command the water itself, calming a surf or raising it; the greatest call down the storm entire. Judge the age by the frill and the eye: a young one's head-crests are soft and its pupils plain, while in the eldest the crests are ridged like a reef and the eyes have gone to solid green with no pupil left to find. Judge it also by manners — the very old are the courteous ones, and the courtesy is not weakness.

lore.summary: Storm giants keep the high cold peaks and the lonely isles, in halls above the cloud or beneath the swell, and they want nothing from you but quiet. Green-skinned, green-haired, taller than a cottage, they read and sing and watch the weather that answers to them. Anger one and the sky replies before the sword does.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — a man's shape built to the scale of a gatehouse, and handsome with it.
Durability: Tremendous. It takes blows all afternoon and considers them afterward.
Defenses: Hide like green stone beneath whatever mail it has forged itself; and nothing binds it — no net, no web, no grasping spell holds a storm giant for a heartbeat.
Speed: Long, unhurried strides; it can float itself and a great weight up a cliff at will, and it breathes water as comfortably as air.
Might: A greatsword the length of a mast, flung stones that land like siege shot, and the lightning — a bolt called out of a clear sky, or a chain of it leaping man to man down the line.
Mind: Wise, thoughtful and widely read. It speaks the common tongue as plainly as its own and would rather use it than the sword.
Disposition: Peaceable, contemplative and mostly good-hearted; slow to anger, and terrible once anger arrives.
Bane: Leave lightning in the bag, it is meat to them, and waste no net or snare — nothing holds them. Their weakness is that they fight fair: they give warning, honour a truce, and will not cut down a man who has laid his arms aside. And a hall is a hall; it cannot follow you into a crawlway.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It opens at distance because it can — a bolt called down, a chain of lightning through your line, stones from the crag above. When you close, the greatsword falls in sweeps that take two men at a stroke, and nothing thrown over it slows it; it walks out of webs and clutching hands as though they were mist. It fights in good order, guards its own, and it will offer terms partway through the business. Take them. It means them.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Bring a song or a book. Payment enough, and safer than gold with these.
• If it warns you, that is not bluster. It is the last free thing you will be given.
• Never open with lightning. It will not so much as blink, and then it will know you for a fool.

sections.title: Parley (open)
sections.body: Knock. I mean it — I climbed three days, called up at the gate, and was given soup and an argument about poetry. They are lonely and they love talk. Come unarmed if your nerve allows, be honest about your errand, and do not lie; they can tell, and a storm giant's disappointment is worse than its anger.

lore.summary: A blank-faced figure of stone, iron and seasoned oak, made to stand between a wizard and the world. It has no mind whatever: it is keyed to an amulet, and whoever wears that amulet it will guard, follow across a kingdom, and take the wounds meant for. Kill the wearer and it simply stands there still, guarding nothing at all.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a broad slab of a figure, half again a tall man's height and heavier than a warhorse.
Durability: It does not tire and it does not bleed. Wounds close over while you watch, and it feels none of them.
Defenses: Banded metal over stone and heartwood; ordinary steel skids away and it wants a truly hard edge to bite. Poison, plague, fear and every trick of the mind slide off a thing that has no mind to trick.
Speed: It walks, steadily, and it never stops walking. It will find its amulet across a whole country and over any ground.
Might: Two hammering fists and nothing clever — it was built to stand still and absorb blows, not to deal them. It may also carry one spell its maker planted inside it.
Mind: None. It hears orders in any tongue and obeys them exactly, which is not at all the same as understanding them.
Disposition: Not malicious. Not anything. It shields the amulet-wearer, takes half of every hurt meant for them, and is otherwise as still as furniture.
Bane: The amulet. Take it and the guardian is yours; destroy it and the thing halts where it stands until another is made. Fighting the guardian itself is the fool's road — go for the cord round the wizard's neck.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It is straightforward to the point of dullness: it plants itself beside whoever wears the amulet and hammers at whatever comes nearest, stepping into blows meant for its master and taking the half of them onto itself. It does not flinch, retreat, feint or improvise, and it cannot be frightened off. If a spell was buried in it, that comes out at the moment its master chose — usually the moment you believe the fight is won.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Do not fight it. Fight the amulet. Everything else is sweat wasted on furniture.
• It closes up as fast as you cut, and blunt work barely marks it. Bring the hardest edge you own.
• Assume its master left a spell asleep inside it, and assume it wakes when you think you have won.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is nobody in there. I have tried; you may as well address a doorpost politely. But mark the difference — it is not wicked, only obedient. The conversation you want is with whoever wears the amulet, and should you get that amulet off them, the thing will turn and guard you instead without a grudge.

lore.summary: Not one beast but two habits of the same beast: the spinner that waits in the dark of its own silk, and the hunter that runs its meat down on open ground. Both are large enough to fill a mine gallery, both are mindless as falling rain, and both carry a venom that unstrings the strength from a man's arms. I have met them in old workings, forest deeps, and the cellars of ruined keeps.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — the body of a pony and the reach of a cartwheel.
Durability: Sturdy, but no sturdier than a great cat; a hard blow tells on it and a second usually settles it.
Defenses: Chitin that turns a glancing cut. Better than that, it cannot be frightened, charmed, cozened or reasoned into flight — there is no mind there to work upon.
Speed: Quick on the flat and quicker still up a sheer wall or across its own ceiling. The hunting sort will outpace a running man.
Might: Not a crusher. The whole of the danger is the bite and what rides in on it — a venom that leaves your sword-arm too weak to lift the sword.
Mind: None. It is a hunger with eight legs and instinct entire.
Disposition: It eats what it catches and catches what comes near. The spinner waits in its web and feels you arrive; the hunter stalks, then springs.
Bane: Fire, and the web itself. Burn the silk and you take away both its ground and its senses. The venom, too, is only venom — a strong constitution or a good draught sees a man through it.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: The spinner never leaves its silk if it can help it: it feels your footfall in the strands, throws a sticky rope from the dark, hauls the fouled man in, and bites him while he is still fighting the threads. The hunter has no such patience — it charges across open floor, leaps the last of the distance, and bears you down under its weight to bite. Neither has any notion of retreat, morale, or mercy. It comes on until it is dead or you are.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Burn the web before you enter it. It hunts by the tremor of the strands — take those and you have blinded it.
• When a friend is being hauled in, cut the strand, not the beast. Faster, and you keep your own footing.
• The venom takes your strength, not your life. Sit down, drink, and wait it out — do not be proud and try to carry your kit home.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is nothing there to talk to. I have tried it — open hands, low voice, the same words that have bought me passage past ogres. It has no ear for meaning and no mind to change. The silence you get back is not refusal. It is absence. Strike first.

lore.summary: A wandering room of clear jelly, as tall as the corridor and as wide, which scours the deep places of everything soft. It has no eye, no malice and no thought — only appetite, and the patience of water. You will not see it until you are inside it. Look instead for what it cannot digest: coins, buckles and bare bones, hanging in still air at the height of a man's chest.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — it fills a passage from wall to wall and from floor to lintel, which is the point of it.
Durability: A great mass of jelly. It soaks up punishment and a blade parts it without much troubling it; you must simply keep cutting.
Defenses: Nearly invisible in still air. It cannot be poisoned, put to sleep, frightened, charmed or fooled by any illusion — you cannot deceive a thing that does not think. Lightning passes through it as through water, and no blow finds a vital spot, for it has none.
Speed: Slow. Slower than a walking man, and it cannot climb after you. Its only ambush is that you never saw it standing there.
Might: The touch numbs, and the numbed are folded inside and dissolved at leisure. It is the paralysis that kills you, not the acid.
Mind: None whatever. It is a stomach that goes for walks.
Disposition: Neither cruel nor hungry in any way you would recognise. It goes down the passage it happens to be in and takes up whatever is loose, corpse or coin or careless man.
Bane: Its own slowness — walk away, and it will not catch you. And mark this: its acid spares metal and stone entirely. Mail, blade and coin come out of it unmarked. Only meat is lost.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It does not fight so much as arrive. It flows forward at its one dull pace, folds over whatever stands in front of it, and holds the man inside while the slime numbs him and the digestion begins. A paralysed man does not drown quickly, which is the true horror of the thing. It will not pursue you far, nor at any speed worth calling pursuit, and it will not choose between targets — it simply continues in the direction it was already going.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Throw dust ahead of you — flour, ash off a torch, anything. It shows the edges of what is not there.
• Coins and belt-buckles floating at chest height are the whole of the warning you are going to get.
• If it takes a companion, cut him free rather than kill the thing. The numbness passes, and the jelly is slow to finish anyone.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Nothing to talk to — less even than the great spiders, for a spider at least wants something. I once stood before one and said my piece for the length of a paternoster, out of a sort of politeness. It came on at exactly the same pace throughout. There is no one home to answer.

lore.summary: A great armoured digger of the deep places, broader than a doorway, with mandibles that shear stone and four eyes set two above two. It swims through rock, drops ceilings on caravans, and eats what falls out of the rubble. Do not mistake it for a beast: it thinks, it chooses which wall to come through, and it speaks a grinding tongue of its own making.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — wider than a door and near as tall, all shoulder and shell.
Durability: Very tough. It carries the punishment of half a dozen good men and keeps digging.
Defenses: A thick plate of chitin over the whole of it. It feels you coming through the stone whether you carry a light or not, and darkness is no hindrance to it at all.
Speed: Ponderous on its feet — you can outpace it in a straight run — but it goes through solid rock nearly as fast as it walks, which makes flight a poorer plan than it sounds.
Might: Two claws that break bones through mail, and mandibles that bite through stone. It does not often need to bite twice.
Mind: As sharp as a slow man, and cunning with it. It picks its wall, sets its collapse, and waits for the sound of a caravan.
Disposition: Cruel and hungry, but patient with it. It much prefers the ambush and the falling ceiling to any honest fight in the open.
Bane: Its eyes. Meet them and your own sword turns on your friends. Refuse them — fight by ear, by touch, with your gaze at its knees — and it is only a strong animal in a hole.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It comes through a wall, never a door, and it looks at you before it does anything else — the four eyes catch a man and set him staggering about swinging at whoever is nearest. Then it wades into the ones still in their senses, claws first, and bites down on whatever it has broken. It fights among its own tunnels by preference, collapsing them behind it to split a party into halves that cannot reach one another, and it will drag its meat back into the rock to eat it out of reach.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Eyes down. Watch the feet, the shadow, the dust off the ceiling — anything but the face.
• It comes through the wall, never the door. Set your back to something it would have to dig a mile to reach.
• Blindfold the hotheads. A man who cannot see it cannot be turned by it, and it swings slower than you fear.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: It has a tongue and words in it, and I have had two words back from one — a name, and a refusal. But it eats folk of our size, and it thinks the way a thing that eats you thinks. Keep your gaze on its feet the whole while you speak. I did not, the first time, and I put a blade through my own guide.

lore.summary: The illithid keeps its cities in the deep dark, ruled by the pooled brain of its elders, and it keeps men the way a farmer keeps cattle — penned, fed, and eaten at need. It devours brains for meat and for what the meat remembers. A squid's head on a scholar's frame, four tentacles, and a mind that will be inside yours before ever its feet have moved.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Medium — no bigger than a tall man, and a good deal slighter.
Durability: Frail. For all the terror of it, the body is the weakest thing it owns; there is less flesh on an illithid than on a scribe.
Defenses: Sorcery slides off it more often than not — a caster of the middling sort can spend a whole fight achieving nothing at all. Its real armour is that you never get close enough to swing.
Speed: Walks like a man, and can rise into the air at a thought, or step clean off the world into another plane the moment the reckoning turns against it.
Might: Almost nothing in the arm. Everything in the head: a silent blast that leaves a rank of armed men standing stunned and slack-jawed, and four tentacles that fasten on a face and take the brain out whole.
Mind: Genius, and it knows it. It reads you, it speaks inside your skull without moving, and it has been planning this conversation since before you came through the door.
Disposition: Cold, patient, and absolute in its own superiority. It keeps thralls, it serves the pooled brain of its elders, and it regards you as livestock that has learned to talk.
Bane: Its body. Close the distance, take the blast on your best-braced men, and cut — it dies as easily as a man dies. And it flees the instant the sum stops favouring it; a fight it is losing is a fight it leaves.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It opens from cover and from darkness with the silent blast, and the front rank of a good company simply stops working. Then it takes the strongest survivor's mind and turns him about to hold the door for it while the tentacles find a stunned face and pull the brain out — done in the open, deliberately, because the sight of it ends most fights on the spot. It is a coward in the honest sense, which is to say a sound tactician: hurt it badly and it will levitate out of reach or step to another plane entirely and be gone.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• It talks inside your head. That is not intimacy, that is a hand in your pocket — hold no thought you would not say aloud.
• Spread out before it says a word. One blast takes everyone standing in a line.
• Free the thralls and it loses half its strength. They are victims, not soldiers, and they know the way out.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: Talk, yes. They are the finest conversationalists in the dark and I have had three long ones and walked away from all three. But you are bargaining with a thing that holds you cattle, and cattle that bargain are a novelty to it, never an equal. Assume it is reading every thought behind your words. It is.

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Mind Blast (Sp): A psionic cone 60 feet long. Anyone caught in the cone must succeed on a DC 17 Will save or be stunned for 3d4 rounds. The save DC is Charisma-based and the ability is the equivalent of a 4th-level spell. Illithids often hunt with it, then drag off one or two stunned victims to feed on.

Psionics (Sp): At will—charm monster (DC 17), detect thoughts (DC 15), levitate, plane shift, suggestion (DC 16). Effective caster level 8th. The save DCs are Charisma-based.

Improved Grab (Ex): On a tentacle hit against a Small, Medium, or Large creature the mind flayer may start a grapple as a free action without provoking an attack of opportunity. Winning the grapple check attaches that tentacle to the foe’s head. Beginning a turn with one tentacle attached, it may attach the rest with a single grapple check; it gains a +2 circumstance bonus per tentacle already attached.

Extract (Ex): A mind flayer that begins its turn with all four tentacles attached and makes a successful grapple check automatically extracts the opponent’s brain, instantly killing it. This is useless against constructs, elementals, oozes, plants, and undead, and is not instantly fatal to many-headed creatures such as ettins and hydras.

Telepathy (Su): A mind flayer can communicate telepathically with any creature within 100 feet that has a language.

lore.summary: A floating sphere of hide and hatred: one great eye above a lamprey's mouth, and ten lesser eyes writhing on stalks above it. Each believes itself the one true and perfect shape in creation, and holds every other thing — its own kin foremost — a flawed draft fit for unmaking. It lairs alone, in caverns bored to suit itself, sleepless and entirely certain.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a sphere the width of two men, hanging at about head height.
Durability: Hardier than it looks. There is a great deal of hide and meat to get through before you reach anything the creature would miss.
Defenses: Its great eye kills magic outright in the wedge before it — spells, wards and enchanted steel all go dead in that cone. Add to that a body that floats out of easy reach and a creature that never sleeps and never lairs in a room with one door.
Speed: It creeps, but it creeps through the air, and it does not tire, and it can hang perfectly still in open space while it works its way through you.
Might: Ten stalks and ten different deaths: sleep, terror, slowing, wounds torn open at a glance, flesh turned to stone, the mind taken and turned about, an unseen hand that lifts a man off his feet — and the two that need no second application, the ray that unmakes you and the one that simply stops the heart.
Mind: Brilliant, and mad with pride in exact proportion. It holds its own shape the single correct shape in creation, and hates its own kind worst of all for getting the details wrong.
Disposition: Paranoid, territorial, sleepless. It lairs alone in caverns it has bored to its own convenience, laced with vertical shafts that a walking man cannot use.
Bane: The great eye and the stalks cannot work the same direction at once — where its dead-magic cone falls, its own rays die with everything else. Take its flank, or stand square in that cone and come at it with plain steel and plain muscle. And cut the stalks: every one you take is a death it no longer owns.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It opens with the great eye wide, drifting forward to strip the wards and enchantments off a party and leave the wizards standing there holding sticks. Then it shuts that eye and rakes the room with the stalks, three at a stroke, spending the killing rays on whoever looked most dangerous while the lesser ones sleep, slow and terrify the rest. It fights in three dimensions and you do not — it will rise above the reach of your polearms, put a shaft or a chasm between you, and pick the party apart at leisure. It never fights fair and never fights where it has not already chosen the ground.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• If you carry no magic, stand where the big eye is looking. Nothing of its own works in there either.
• Cut the stalks. Every one you take is a death it will never deal again.
• Never fight it in its own cavern. Those shafts are bored for a thing that floats, and you do not.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: Talk to one and you may yet live — they are vain, and vanity wants an audience. I kept one in conversation the better part of an hour, praising the symmetry of it, and left with my skin on. But know what you are flattering: a thing that holds every other shape an error. When it kills you it will not be treachery. It will be tidiness.

sections.body: Dire — A dire quarry

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Eye Rays (Su): Each of the ten small eyes fires one magical ray per round as a free action. In one round it can aim only three rays into any single 90-degree arc (up, forward, backward, left, right, down). Each ray resembles a spell cast by a 13th-level caster but follows the rules for a ray. Range 150 feet, save DC 17, Charisma-based.

Ray — Charm Monster: Will DC 17 negates, otherwise the target is affected as the spell. Used early to confuse the opposition; the charmed target is told to restrain a comrade or stand aside.

Ray — Charm Person: Will DC 17 negates, otherwise the target is affected as the spell. Used the same way as the charm monster ray.

Ray — Disintegrate: Fortitude DC 17 negates, otherwise the target is affected as the spell. Aimed at any foe the beholder considers a real threat.

Ray — Fear: As the spell, but affecting a single creature; Will DC 17 negates. Used early against warriors and other powerful creatures to break up the opposition.

Ray — Finger of Death: Fortitude DC 17 or the target is slain as the spell; on a successful save the target still takes 3d6+13 points of damage. Used to eliminate dangerous foes quickly.

Ray — Flesh to Stone: Fortitude DC 17 negates, otherwise the target is affected as the spell. Aimed at enemy spellcasters, or at any creature the beholder finds interesting — the statue later decorates its lair.

Ray — Inflict Moderate Wounds: As the spell, dealing 2d8+10 points of damage, Will DC 17 for half.

Ray — Sleep: As the spell, except that it affects a single creature regardless of how mighty that creature is; Will DC 17 negates. Used on warriors and other physically powerful foes, since waking them costs the party time.

Ray — Slow: As the spell, except that it affects a single creature; Will DC 17 negates. Often aimed at the same creature targeted by a disintegrate, flesh to stone, or finger of death ray, to hamper a foe those rays failed to remove.

Ray — Telekinesis: The beholder can move objects or creatures weighing up to 325 pounds, as the telekinesis spell; Will DC 17 resists.

Antimagic Cone (Su): The central eye continually produces a 150-foot cone of antimagic straight ahead, functioning as antimagic field (caster level 13th). All magical and supernatural powers and effects within the cone are suppressed, including the beholder’s own eye rays. Once each round it chooses its facing and whether the cone is active (it deactivates it by shutting the central eye).

Flight (Ex): A beholder’s body is naturally buoyant, letting it fly at a speed of 20 feet as a free action and granting it a permanent feather fall effect (as the spell) with personal range.

All-Around Vision (Ex): A beholder’s many eyes grant it a +4 racial bonus on Spot and Search checks, and it cannot be flanked.

Source Note: Not part of the SRD (product identity). Reconstructed from the Monster Manual v.3.5, p. 25–26.

lore.summary: Eight legs, dull brown above and yellow beneath, and slower than a well-fed hound — and it kills you by looking. The basilisk keeps to warm desert rock and dry scrub, lying motionless for days on end, taking whatever wanders past: hares, birds, lizards, fools. Some wear a short curved horn upon the snout. Find one and look for its kin; they den in colonies.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Man-sized, but squat and low to the ground, with a tail near as long again as the body.
Durability: Tougher than its bulk promises; it absorbs punishment without hurry or complaint.
Defenses: Thick pebbled hide, and eyes that need no light to find you. Nothing else — it has never needed anything else.
Speed: Wretchedly slow. Its cold blood begrudges every step, and a man who flees gets a halfhearted pursuit at worst.
Might: A heavy crushing bite for anything foolish enough to come within reach — but the bite is an afterthought. The eyes are the weapon.
Mind: Beast-dull. It hunts, it basks, it waits. There is nothing behind those eyes but appetite.
Disposition: Neither cruel nor kind. A patient ambusher that lets the world walk into its range and then looks up.
Bane: Its own gaze cannot harm it — the mirror trick is a tavern tale, and the men who believed it are standing in the desert still. What works is duller: avert your eyes, or shut them outright and fight by ear. Then walk away. It will not chase far.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It does not charge. It lies still among the rocks until something crosses into its range, and then it looks — and looks again, and keeps looking, every heartbeat of the fight, whether you are attending to it or not. Only when you blunder within reach of those jaws does it trouble itself to bite. Run, and it may follow a few paces out of habit before settling back down to wait for something less trouble.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Blindfold. Cloth, not your fingers. It is slow enough that fighting by ear will serve.
• Its statues stand where it left them. A garden of screaming men means a den — and likely more than one tenant.
• A polished shield is for watching it by, not for killing it with. Mirrors do nothing. Ask the men I buried.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: None. I have tried, for the sake of having tried, and got what a hare gets. It has the wit of a hound with none of the affection, no tongue of its own, and no interest at all in yours. Shut your eyes, put a spear through it, and be about your business.

lore.summary: A cockerel with a lizard's tail, a bat's wings, and the temper of a wasp. The male carries comb and wattles like any farmyard bird; the female, far rarer, goes bare-headed. It flies badly and lands worse, and it will go at anything it reckons a threat to itself or its nest. Temperate grassland is its country. Absurd, every inch — and it has ended better men than me.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Small — a stout fowl, no heavier than a fat goose, and it looks every bit as ridiculous.
Durability: Frail. A good blow ends it, and a poor blow often will.
Defenses: None worth the name. It is quick and awkward to catch square in the air, and that is the whole of its protection.
Speed: It waddles on the ground and flies clumsily — but clumsy is not slow, and it will be at your face before you have finished deciding.
Might: Its bite could scarcely bruise a child. Its bite also turns a grown man to stone where he stands. Both things are true.
Mind: Bird-dull, and vicious with it.
Disposition: Fiercely territorial. It attacks whatever it takes for a threat to itself or its lair, and a flock will crowd and muddle you, flying full into your face.
Bane: The curse rides on the bite, and the bite must find flesh. Gauntlets, a closed helm, a hood — leave it nothing to reach and it is only an angry chicken. Then kill it quickly; a long stick will do.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It comes low and fast, or a flock does, all at once, beating about your head to confuse you while one of them looks for skin. There is no cunning in it whatever. There is only the bite, and the bite is sufficient. They will fly bodily into a man's face to reach his eyes and his mouth, which is where the skin is bare, and they know it in the way birds know things.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Gauntlets and a closed helm. It needs one bite on bare flesh and it only gets what you leave out.
• Long weapons. A staff, a boar spear — anything that keeps that beak an arm's length off.
• They cannot turn one another to stone, but a basilisk's look takes them like anything else. I keep a stone one by my door. It holds it open handsomely.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never. It is a bird with a hen's wit and a wasp's temper, and no more speech in it than a hen has. I once set down bread for a flock, in a fit of hopefulness. They ate the bread. Then they came for me. Cover your skin and be quick about it.

lore.summary: A bear's body, a bear's temper doubled and soured, and the head of a great owl set atop it — beak, ear tufts, and eyes rimmed red with a madness that is not natural, because the beast itself is not. Some wizard made the first of them, and the temperate forests have paid for it ever since. It attacks anything larger than a mouse, on sight, and does not stop.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a full-grown male stands head and shoulders over a tall man and outweighs a warhorse.
Durability: Enormously hardy. It goes on tearing at you long past the point where an honest bear would lie down and think better of it.
Defenses: A thick coat over thicker hide, and a nose that finds you through a night of rain. It has no guile and has never wanted any.
Speed: Quick over open ground, and quicker through timber — quicker than you, certainly, over any distance that matters.
Might: Two clawed arms that take hold and do not let go, and a beak that sets to work on whatever they are holding.
Mind: Beast-dull, but carrying a spite in it that no honest bear has ever had.
Disposition: Ill-tempered past all reason. It comes at anything bigger than a mouse the moment it sees it, and it fights to the death every single time.
Bane: Great as it is, its arms are short — it must come right up against you to use them at all. Keep it at a set spear's length, or across water, and it has nothing. And it never flees, which means it never learns.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It closes at once and grabs. A claw hooks you, the arms come round, and thereafter it is a question of whether your ribs or your harness give way first while the beak works at your face. Once it has hold of a man it will not be distracted onto another. It fights to the death, always, without exception — and a pack of them will simply all do this at the same time, from different sides.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Spears, and set them in the earth. Its arms are shorter than they look. Make it come to the point.
• Once it takes hold it lets go for nothing short of dying. Give one companion no job but prying.
• It never runs. Use that — lead it onto a pit, a rope, a bad slope. It will follow you into anything at all.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is none to be had. I have talked a hungry bear off a kill; I have never talked an owlbear off anything. Whatever the wizard bred out of it, he bred out the part that hesitates. No tongue, no fear, no interest in your bread. Kill it, or be elsewhere before it scents you.

lore.summary: Half again a tall man's height, green and rubbery, hunched forward with sagging shoulders and arms that drag the ground when it runs — and it runs well, for all that it looks broken. The cold mountains are its country, alone or in small gangs. It regrows what you cut away in the time it takes to eat a meal, and it is always about to eat a meal.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large and ill-made — taller than any man, all uneven gait and trailing arms, and far more agile than that gait leads you to hope.
Durability: The worst you will meet at its station. Wounds close while you watch. Cut a limb away and it grows back, or it picks the thing up off the ground and presses it back on.
Defenses: Rubbery hide, a keen nose, and eyes that see deep into full dark. But its true armour is simply that nothing you do to it stays done.
Speed: Fast afoot, tireless, and it will chase you the whole night if it has your scent.
Might: Raking claws and a bite — and if both claws take hold at once it hauls you in and tears. That is the wound that kills men. The scratches are nothing.
Mind: Dim, but not witless. It has the giants' tongue and enough sense to use it, and it can be bargained with by a man who understands the bargain will not hold.
Disposition: Chaotic, cruel, and hungry without end. It flings itself at the nearest living thing without a moment's thought for what that costs it.
Bane: Fire and acid, and nothing else. Cut it, crush it, shoot it as you like — it comes back. Burn the wound, or bathe it in something that eats flesh, and it stays down. Carry oil, and carry more than you think you want.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It launches itself at whoever stands nearest and flails, with no plan whatever and no regard for what it takes back. Having no fear of death, it does not give ground, does not favour a wound, does not flinch. Set a wall of fire in front of one and it will try to come round the flames rather than withdraw. When both claws find purchase it drags you against itself and rends, and that is where men die — not to the flailing, but to the moment it gets a proper grip.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Oil and a lit torch, always. Steel alone only makes it angry and briefly shorter.
• Burn the pieces where they fall. A hand left lying will find its way back to the arm, and it does not take long.
• It does not flee and it does not tire. If you cannot burn it, do not begin.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: Talk is possible. Trust is not. It has the giants' tongue and wit enough to use it, and meat buys you a hearing — I have bought passage with a mule, twice, and both times it came after us anyway once the mule was gone. Speak from high ground. Keep the fire lit. Never turn your back on a hungry bargain.

lore.summary: A great dull brute in badly cured hides, half again a man's height and broad as a doorway, and you will smell it long before you see it. Ogres hold the temperate hills, alone or in gangs and ragged bands, and they live entirely by taking — cattle, carts, travellers, and each other's shares. They are cowardly in a manner easily mistaken for cunning.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — head and shoulders above a tall man, and heavy with it.
Durability: Thickly built and no easy thing to put down, but nothing uncanny about it. It dies the way a bull dies.
Defenses: A coat of hides over a hide of its own, and eyes made for the dark. Slow to react, though, and easily caught wrong-footed.
Speed: Longer in the stride than you would credit, especially once it sheds that armour and runs. Do not count on outpacing one across open hill.
Might: Prodigious. A club like a fence post, swung by shoulders that can stove in a barred door. One good blow ends most men.
Mind: Dull. It speaks the giants' tongue; the rare brighter specimen has picked up enough Common to haggle and to threaten, in that order.
Disposition: Greedy, cruel, and lazy in equal measure. It wants your goods and your food, and it does not want a fight it might lose.
Bane: No discipline and no patience. A band fights as a crowd of separate brutes — nobody guards a flank, nobody covers a fellow, and one will break off to rifle a fallen pack while his kin are still bleeding. Break the loudest one loudly and the rest lose the thread.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It would rather not fight fairly at all: ambush from above the road, rocks and javelins first to soften you, then the club. The throwing is poor and mostly noise — stand your ground through it. Even a full band comes at you as a mob of individuals, each swinging at whoever happens to be nearest, with no thought of holding a line, and any one of them will abandon the fight the moment there is loot on the ground worth having.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Ale. In earnest. A cask buys more road than a drawn sword, and they never once think to ask why you were carrying it.
• They ambush from above. Check the ridge and check the rocks before you check the road.
• Fell the loud one first. An ogre band has no plan beyond the loud one.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: Yes — carefully. It has the giants' tongue and it wants what you carry rather more than it wants a fight it might lose. Show strength first, then show a toll: salt meat, ale, coin. I bought a whole road from a band with a cask and a lie. Pay, keep walking, and never camp where they watched you pay.

lore.summary: Two heads on one filthy body, and neither of them cares for the other. Ettins stalk the cold hills by night — better than twice a man's height of grey grime that has never once been washed — a morningstar swinging in either fist. Look for the brown bears they keep as hounds, and for the orc and goblin camps that squat under their protection.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — better than twice a man's height and heavier than a cart-horse, the two heads set straight upon shoulders with barely a neck between.
Durability: Thick with muscle under the crust of filth. It soaks up wounds and keeps swinging long after a lesser thing would sit down in the heather.
Defenses: Hide gone leathery from a lifetime unwashed, and stitched skins worn over that. No cleverness in its defence — only bulk, and a great deal of it.
Speed: Long-legged and quick across broken hill ground, though its heaped armour costs it something. It will run a man down uphill.
Might: Enormous. A morningstar in each fist, and because each head drives its own arm there is no fumbling between them — both blows come in as true as one. It throws javelins that would spit a horse.
Mind: Dull as a stone, but not stupid in a fight: it chooses its ground, lays its ambush, and waits. And two heads make it wretchedly hard to creep upon — something up there is always listening.
Disposition: Vicious, foul-tempered and unpredictable. A night hunter that takes whatever is walking, and you are walking.
Bane: The two heads. They share a body but never a mind, and they bicker without ceasing. Give them something to quarrel over — terms, plunder, which of you to eat first — and the arms slow while the mouths work. Failing that, it is a clumsy thing: step aside and it puts its whole weight into nothing at all.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It does not roar and charge. It lies behind rock or scrub and lets you come, opening with javelins if it has them, then rising to swing both morningstars at once — which is the whole of its trick and a very good one, for two heads mean two full-strength arms and no clumsiness between the blows. Once it is in, it stays in: it does not withdraw, does not tire, and does not leave off until every enemy on his feet is off them. Put down its bears first, or they will hold you while it works.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• It owns no tongue — only Orc, Goblin and Giant, badly mixed. Every one of the three you lack doubles the labour of being understood.
• Never try to slip past one in the dark. One head sleeps; the other is listening to your boots.
• Set the heads to arguing. I have watched an ettin stand quarrelling with itself while I walked out of its cave.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: They have no speech of their own — only a mangled soup of Orc, Goblin and Giant. I have made myself understood twice, and both times it was sweating work. Speak to both heads. Address the one and the other takes offence, and the offended head has an arm.

lore.summary: A ruddy brute half again as tall as a tall man, wrapped in stinking layered hides it has never washed nor mended — it simply piles new skins over the rotted ones. Hill giants hold the high rocky ground of the temperate uplands, raiding farm and road for cattle and coin, and they keep dire wolves the way a shepherd keeps dogs.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — half again a tall man's height and near half a ton of him, most of it shoulder.
Durability: Immensely stout. It has the constitution of an ox and takes a beating like one, and keeps its feet long past the point of sense.
Defenses: Hide thick as boiled leather beneath crude piled furs. Nothing subtle, nothing clever — but very hard to put down.
Speed: Heavy-footed and ungainly, yet its stride eats ground, and it climbs rock far better than you would credit of a thing that shape.
Might: Prodigious. A club the size of a roof-beam, and it will smash a shield or snap a good blade on purpose if the notion takes it. It throws boulders, too, and throws them a long way.
Mind: Very dim. It knows raiding, eating, and where it stands in the tribe, and little else. It speaks Giant, and speaks it badly.
Disposition: A bully, plain and simple. Greedy, reckless, and cruel to anything smaller than itself — which is nearly everything.
Bane: It wants the high rocks and the boulders it can drop from them; take that away and it is only a slow, clumsy thing that swings and misses. Do not answer its stones with stones of your own — it plucks them out of the air and sends them back. Get close, keep to its flanks, and make it turn.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It opens from a high outcrop, flinging rocks down while you labour up the slope towards it. When you finally arrive it charges through your line to bowl over the small ones, then plants its feet and simply swings, again and again, breaking shields and swords along with the arms behind them. It does not manoeuvre and it does not retreat. Its dire wolves come in from the sides while it holds you in front — that is the whole of the tribe's strategy, and it works often enough.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Do not throw its own rocks back. It catches them. I have had a boulder returned with interest.
• Every hill giant fight is really a fight for the high ground. Win that one first.
• Kill the dire wolves before the giant. The giant is slow; the wolves are not.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: They speak Giant, poorly, and understand three things: food, tribute, and a bigger fist. I bought passage off a raiding party once with four barrels of salted beef and a keg of ale. They took the goods and let us by — and would have taken us as well, had we looked the cheaper meal.

lore.summary: A distant, dim cousin to the true dragons: a long body of dark brown scale, half of it tail, borne on two legs and two great wings with no arms between them. No breath, no hoard-craft, no cunning — only speed out of the sun and a barb at the tail's end whose venom kills a grown man while he is still arguing about it. Warm hills and high crags; alone, or in mated pairs.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a body as long as a river-boat with a wingspan half again wider, and fully half that length is tail.
Durability: Solidly built and thickly scaled. It takes a great deal more killing than a beast of its bulk has any right to.
Defenses: Heavy scale, keen eyes, a keener nose — it smells you coming up a valley. And like all its dragon kin, no spell will lull it to sleep nor lock its limbs.
Speed: Wretched on the ground; it waddles like a fat goose. Aloft it is very fast and utterly clumsy — it flies like a thrown spear, and turns like one.
Might: Talons that close on a man and carry him off, jaws that take the leg from a horse — but the tail settles the argument. The sting comes over the shoulder while the claws hold you, and its venom wastes the flesh, then rests a while and wastes it again.
Mind: Dull as a hound and twice as bold. It has the tongue of dragons and rarely troubles with it; a hiss, or a growl like a bull alligator, serves for most of its conversation.
Disposition: Aggressive without a shred of judgment. It attacks anything that does not plainly outmatch it, which is how the greater part of them die.
Bane: It flies like a hurled stone — fast, straight, and unable to turn. Fight it under a canopy, in a gorge, in a hall, anywhere the sky is small, and it must come down and waddle. And carry a remedy for venom before you carry anything else: the sting has killed far more men than the claws ever have.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It hunts by eye from a great height and comes down out of the sun in one long stoop, raking with the talons as it passes and wheeling for another run. When it means to finish the business it takes hold instead — the claws close, the grip locks, and the tail whips over the shoulder to sting you again and again while you hang there kicking. It is far too stupid to know when it is losing, and will press an attack any sensible beast would have broken off, which is the only reason a party of moderate men ever kills one.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• No forelimbs. Everything it does it does with feet, jaws or that tail — and it is always the tail.
• Take it into a gorge, a wood, a hall. It flies fast and turns like a barge.
• Carry the antitoxin, and carry it where a man with one working arm can reach it.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: It has the tongue of dragons and the wit of a hunting dog. Words alone will not turn it; words from a place it can see is stronger will. Twice I have sent one off with the Draconic for mine, shouted from a ledge it could not reach. It is not hoard-proud. It wants meat, and prefers meat that does not shout back.

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: Do not wait for it to become something grander — that is the mercy of the breed. A wyvern hatches, hardens, grows, and then simply is: it gains no breath, no spell-craft, no long slow cunning, and the eldest is only a bolder version of the youngest. The very greatest never stop growing, mind, and a truly ancient one can reach a bulk that shades a field, with a tail thick as a barrel and a stoop you feel in the ground. Judge its years by the scale — the young are near black and glossy, the old are weathered grey and dulled, the wing-membranes patched and holed and pale along the trailing edge, the sting worn blunt and grown back crooked. Judge nothing at all by its temper. They are equally rash at every age; the old ones have merely been lucky longer.

lore.summary: It looks like a heap of rotted vegetation left lying in a marsh, and that is precisely what it intends. A shambler is a thinking, meat-eating plant — a squat sprawling mass that weighs as much as a wagon and team — and it lies among the reeds until something walks near enough, then rises on two thick limbs and folds them round you. Temperate marshes, always alone.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — broad rather than tall. Reared up it stands only about a man's height, but it sprawls wide and weighs as much as a loaded cart with the horses still in the traces.
Durability: Frightening. There is nothing in it to burst and nothing vital to find; you do not wound a shambler, you dismantle it, layer by rotting layer.
Defenses: A dense mat of creeper, root and rot that turns a blade aside. No poison touches it, no terror moves it, no spell that clouds a mind finds one to cloud — and with no throat to open and no heart to pierce, a lucky thrust is worth no more than a clumsy one.
Speed: Slow and lumbering on land, and as much at home swimming as walking. It does not chase. It has never needed to.
Might: Two great armlike limbs that batter, and then catch. Once it has hold it draws you into the mass and crushes, and the crushing is worse than the battering by a very wide margin.
Mind: Dim, but genuinely thinking — cunning enough to pick the ford you must use and lie still beside it for days. It has no speech and no use for any.
Disposition: A patient ambusher, neither cruel nor kind. It is hungry; you are meat that has walked into the marsh.
Bane: Steel and cold do honest work on it. Fire burns it too, though it shrugs off a good deal of any burning — a torch will not do the labour of an axe. But never lightning: it drinks a bolt whole and takes no hurt at all, swelling stronger and hardier for an hour after. I have watched a hedge-wizard feed one to a size it had no business reaching. Beyond that, it is slow and it is always alone. Stay clear of its arms and you may simply walk away.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It waits. Sunk into the wet mat of the marsh it is not a creature at all, only more marsh, and it will hold that stillness as long as its hunger permits. When you are inside its reach it comes up and strikes with both limbs at once — and if both find you, it does not strike again. It gathers you in and begins to squeeze, and it will not let go while you have breath in you. Cut at the arms. Do not go hunting for a heart; there is not one to find.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Never lightning. Not a spark, not a wand, not a storm — you are only feeding it.
• Fire helps but does not decide it. Bring the axe as well as the torch.
• It is slow, and it is always alone. If it is not your quarry, step off the bank and go the long way round.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is nothing to say to it. It thinks, after a fashion — enough to choose the crossing you must use and lie beside it — but it has no tongue, no ear for speech, and no interest in you that is not appetite. I tried, in Sylvan and Druidic both, from a safe rock. It never so much as shifted. Strike first, or better, be elsewhere.

lore.summary: A tree that watches you, and considers, and can walk. An oak or elm or ash grown taller than a village roof, with a face in the bark and legs that close together into a trunk when it stands still — and standing still it is a tree, and you will not find it. Treants keep the deep temperate forests, alone or in groves of a handful. They are good folk. Give them no cause.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — a full-grown forest tree that walks, with a trunk you could not put your arms around and a reach that takes in half a road.
Durability: Vast, old, and slow to fail. Wood does not bleed, and it has a very great deal of wood.
Defenses: Bark like plate. Point and thrust glance off it — only a good edge swung with weight behind it bites, and even then there is a fearful amount of biting to do. No poison touches it, no terror moves it, no charm reaches whatever serves it for a mind.
Speed: Deliberate. A man may outwalk it on open ground — but not in its own wood, where it wakes the trees standing in front of you.
Might: Two limbs that come down like felling timber, and it will walk straight over the small and the fallen. Against doors, walls, wagons and palisades there is nothing worse in the world; it takes a gate apart the way you take apart a loaf.
Mind: Sharp. Old, patient, well-spoken and shrewd, and it reads a man's intent rather better than most men do. It has its own tongue, and Common and Sylvan besides, and enough of every other speech to say get away from my trees.
Disposition: Peaceable, good-hearted, and the sole warden of its wood. It watches a long while before it acts. Very slow to anger; very hard to stop afterwards.
Bane: Fire. It does not merely suffer flame — it burns worse than any living thing ought to, and so do the trees it wakes, for they share the failing. Which is exactly why fire is the one thing you must never bring into that wood, even by accident. A good woodsman's edge will also bite where a spear-point only slides.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It watches from cover first, and its cover is perfect — it is a tree until it decides otherwise, and the deciding is the first you know of it. Then it comes out at a charge and walks through you, trampling whoever goes down, and brings both limbs down like felled timber on whoever is still standing. Pressed hard, it wakes the wood: trees haul their own roots free and come on, and they fight as it fights. It goes for your works before your people — the wagon, the bridge, the camp gate, the mill — because it knows what you came for and means to take that from you first.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Axes shouldered, fires cold, and ask leave before you cut. That is very nearly the whole of it.
• Standing still it is a tree, and a convincing one. You have walked past more of them than you know.
• It breaks the wagon and the gate before it breaks you. That is a warning being given to you — take it as one and give ground.

sections.title: Parley (open)
sections.body: Talk. Always talk. Few great powers of the wild will hear a man out and answer him fairly in his own tongue, and this one will. Come with axes shouldered and fires cold, ask leave for every tree you take, and it may see you through the wood itself. Bring flame in and the conversation is finished before you open your mouth.
